newsitem.title: LAOS: Laos says ASEAN bid with Burma, Cambodia on track.
newsitem.headline: Laos says ASEAN bid with Burma, Cambodia on track.

text.p: Recent troubles in Cambodia and Burma are not expected to derail the imminent entry of the two countries and Laos into the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), a top Lao official said on Monday.
Asked whether he was worried at the possibility of delay, Sayakane Sisouvong, deputy director general of the ASEAN Department, said: "We are not concerned at all."
"We have been tracing the record of ASEAN decisions in the past and we know they have a good record. There has not been a change when things have been decided," he told Reuters in an interview.

Laos, which is scheduled to join ASEAN this year at the same time as fellow observer nations Cambodia and Burma, has been working hard to met the requirements for entry into the regional group, said Sisouvong. ASEAN currently groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Compared with Cambodia, which is embroiled in political turmoil, and Burma, which is trying to shrug off U.S. opposition to its ASEAN bid, communist Laos appears to have relatively few problems.
But Romeo Reyes, a senior economist for the U.N. Development Programme, said the problems of Burma and Cambodia had probably slowed Laos' entry into ASEAN.
"Cambodia and Burma have delayed Laos. Laos could have been a member with Vietnam in 1995 if the other two hadn't registered their interest and been grouped together," he said.
A Western diplomat agreed, but Sisouvong said Laos would not have been ready to join ASEAN in 1995.
Now Laos is ready and is likely to continue the process of economic opening and growth that began with its 1986 New Economic Mechanism.
While the country has met the technical requirements of entry, some problems remain, Sisouvong said.
First, there is the hefty cost of entry and attendance at dozens of meetings for a country with a per capita annual gross domestic product of only $385.
Then there is the education gap. Laos lacks strong human resources and a large, skilled work force, said Sisouvong.
The country also is heavily dependent on customs revenues, said Reyes, which provide almost half of the state budget. ASEAN membership means those tariffs will have to be lowered soon.
But unlike Cambodia and Burma, Laos has political stability -- an advantage bolstered by a pragmatic outlook, said analysts.
"They don't do crazy things when they land investors. They're very realistic," said one diplomat. "It helps that they know who they are and what they have."
